hints: Notice the question asks for a derivation, so check the starting definitions for $power$ and $work\ done$ in each option.
Recall that velocity is displacement divided by time taken, not distance divided by time taken, and work done uses displacement in the direction of the force.
Check which option correctly substitutes $force \times displacement$ into $work\ done / time\ taken$ and simplifies to $force \times velocity$.
walkthrough: Start with the definitions: $power = work\ done / time\ taken$ and, for a constant force in the direction of motion, $work\ done = force \times displacement$.
Substitute the work expression into the power expression to get $power = (force \times displacement) / time\ taken$.
Regroup the right-hand side as $force \times (displacement / time\ taken)$ while keeping force constant.
Recognise that $displacement / time\ taken = velocity$, so the expression becomes $power = force \times velocity$.
This correct chain using displacement, not distance and not division, is option A.

options.A: Uses $work\ done = force \times displacement$ and $power = work\ done / time\ taken$, so $power = force \times (displacement/time\ taken) = force \times velocity$.
options.B: Uses distance instead of displacement, so it mixes scalar distance and speed with vector force and velocity and does not give a correct vector derivation.
options.C: Starts from the wrong $work\ done = force/displacement$, so the substitution and rearrangement to $force/velocity$ are invalid.
options.D: Starts from the wrong $work\ done = force/distance$, so the substitution and rearrangement to $force/velocity$ are invalid.
